blocks.text: **The problem.** Given a **circular** array `nums` — after the last element comes the first one again — return the **next greater number** for every element: the first number bigger than it when you walk forward, wrapping around the end. If no number in the whole circle is bigger, the answer is **-1**. Values may repeat.

blocks.alt: The numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 3 arranged in a circle. Walking forward from the last 3, you wrap around past 1, 2 and 3 to reach 4, so its next greater number is 4. 4 is the largest, so its answer is -1.

blocks.code:
Input:  nums = [1, 2, 1]
Output: [2, -1, 2]      the last 1 wraps around to find 2

Input:  nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 3]
Output: [2, 3, 4, -1, 4]

blocks.text: This is **Next Greater Element** with one twist: the search may **wrap around**. Without the wrap, the last element would always get -1.
1. Brute force: walk forward around the circle
For each index, look at the next `n - 1` positions, wrapping with `% n`, and stop at the first bigger number.
**Time O(n²), space O(1)** beyond the output. A decreasing array like `[5, 4, 3, 2, 1]` makes almost every scan go all the way round.
2. Optimal: unroll the circle into a line

A circle is awkward, but a **line** we already know how to handle. Write the array **twice** in a row: `[1, 2, 1]` becomes `[1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 1]`. Now "walk forward and wrap" is just "walk forward" — every element of the first copy can see all of the others to its right. Run the ordinary next-greater stack over the doubled array and keep the first `n` answers.

blocks.alt: The array 1, 2, 1 written twice: 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 1. The last 1 of the first copy now has the second copy to its right, and finds 2 there.

elements.text: the last 1 finds 2 in the copy
elements.originalText: the last 1 finds 2 in the copy

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(n)** — but the doubled array, the double-length answer array and a stack of up to 2n indexes all cost extra memory.
3. Best solution: two laps, no copy

We never need the copy itself — index `i` of the doubled array is just `nums[i % n]`. So loop `i` from `0` to `2n - 1` and read `nums[i % n]`. One more saving: in the second lap every element has already been pushed once, so it only **answers** waiting indexes — it never needs to wait again.

blocks.alt: Two laps over the same array. Lap 1, i from 0 to n - 1: every index is pushed and may answer earlier ones. Lap 2, i from n to 2n - 1, reading nums[i % n]: indexes are no longer pushed; each element only answers indexes still waiting from lap 1.

blocks.caption: Watch lap 2 answer the indexes that were still waiting after lap 1.

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(n)** for the stack only. Each index is pushed once (in lap 1) and popped at most once. Why push **indexes**, not values? Values can repeat — `[1, 2, 1]` has two 1s — and the answer must be written into the right slot.

rows.approach: Brute force: walk forward around the circle
rows.timeWhy: Each of the **n** numbers may walk **all the way round**.

rows.approach: Optimal: unroll the circle into a line
rows.timeWhy: A monotonic stack over the **2n** doubled array: each index pushed and popped once.

items: **One element** — nothing else in the circle: -1.
**All equal**, like `[5, 5, 5]` — nothing is strictly greater: all -1.
**The maximum appears twice** — both copies get -1.
**Strictly decreasing** — every element except the first finds its answer only by wrapping round.
